item.title: Tankers continue to burn in the Middle East despite hopes for de-escalation - WNWN-FM
item.summary: An image captured by the ⁠European Union's Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellite on Sunday showed a large cloud of black smoke at the same location. It ...
item.page_text:
(Corrects in paragraph 4 to ‘a Navig8 tanker’, removing reference to ‘Navig8 Messi’; it was not clear which Navig8 tanker was shown)
Nov 10 (Reuters) – Despite market bets on a de-escalation in the Iran war, new evidence has emerged in recent days of strikes on tankers in the Strait of ​Hormuz and on energy infrastructure in the Middle East.
On Tuesday, crude prices hit two-month lows ‌after US officials downplayed the need for additional military action against Iran, with analysts noting President Donald Trump’s more conciliatory tone since the Republicans’ defeat in the November 3 midterm elections.
However, there is little sign of attacks abating in November, after 37 ships were attacked in October, the highest monthly total since the start of the war, according to data from the Washington Institute ‌for Near ​East Policy.
Videos posted on social media on Sunday and verified by Reuters ⁠showed a Navig8 tanker on fire ⁠near the coast of Oman. An image captured by the European Union’s Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellite on Sunday showed a large cloud of black smoke at the same location.
It was one of three tankers hit on Sunday for using “unauthorised routes” through the strait, Iranian state broadcaster IRIB reported, citing the Islamic Revolutionary ​Guard Corps Navy.
The vessel is managed by Navig8, majority owned by ADNOC Logistics & Services. Neither replied to emailed Reuters requests for comment.
At the same time, US forces continued to enforce a naval blockade of Iranian ⁠ports. In the latest incident, a US military aircraft fired on ⁠and disabled a St Kitts-flagged cargo vessel that tried to depart regional waters ​after visiting an Iranian port on Saturday, US Central Command said.
Attacks in the strait have caused environmental damage, with ​oil leaking from damaged tankers. A video shared on social media on Monday, and verified ‌by Reuters, showed oil reaching the shores of Oman, while satellite imagery showed oil spills off the coast of Oman and UAE. The Omani government did not respond to Reuters request on Tuesday for comment on the video of oil reaching Omani shores.
Elsewhere in the region, energy infrastructure and civilian facilities have also come under attack. ⁠Iran and its regional allies have struck targets including the offices of Saudi Aramco, the world’s largest oil company. Video verified by Reuters showed damage to Aramco’s office building in Riyadh, following Houthi-claimed missile strikes on November 8.
The ⁠Saudi Energy Ministry said that a ‌building belonging to Aramco in Riyadh had been targeted in an attempted attack, ⁠with debris causing limited damage to the building with no injuries or fatalities.
The ​International Maritime ‌Organization has confirmed 130 incidents, most of them attacks, in the region ​since the conflict ⁠began in late February, with at least 25 seafarers killed.
Another tanker was struck northeast of Oman’s Lima, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said on Tuesday. UKMTO did not say who struck it.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy said in a separate statement that two tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines on the “unauthorized route” in the strait.
(Reporting by Catherine Cartier in Beirut, Arthur Wei in Beijing and Edward Carron in London; Writing by Nerijus Adomaitis; Editing ​by Tomasz Janowski, Alexandra Hudson)

item.title: Water Surges Into Navajo Reservoir
item.summary: Rounds of heavy rain in the U.S. Southwest flooded rivers and rapidly raised New Mexico’s second-largest reservoir.
item.page_text:
Rounds of heavy rain in the U.S. Southwest flooded rivers and rapidly raised New Mexico’s second-largest reservoir.
Back-to-back extreme rain events inundated the Four Corners region of the U.S. Southwest in late October and early November 2026. The storms alleviated short-term drought conditions in the Southwest but caused river levels to spike to record or near-record levels in places, triggering damaging floods.
One effect of the heavy rains detected by satellites was the rapid rise of water levels in Navajo Reservoir. The change is visible in the images above, acquired on September 20 (left) and November 7 (right) with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 . In that time, the lake in northern New Mexico and southern Colorado rose by nearly 60 feet (18 meters), according to data from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. (Note that the Bureau of Reclamation decreased releases from Navajo Dam on September 16 and 17.)
On November 7, the reservoir stood at its highest level since August 2019 and at 108 percent of the average capacity for that date. That contrasts with September 20, when it held just 60 percent of its average capacity. Due to snow drought across the West in winter 2025-26, the lake saw relatively little growth in the spring, when snowmelt often raises water levels.
The San Juan, Piedra, and other rivers swelled with runoff amid the wet weather. Pagosa Springs, Colorado, a town along the San Juan River about 40 miles (64 kilometers) northeast of the lake, was especially hard-hit by flooding. In the first round of rain, 5.05 inches (12.8 centimeters) fell in the town, and on October 23 the river reached major flood stage . After more rain, the river spiked again on November 1, this time nearly to the record level set in 1911 during a devastating flood . Officials issued evacuation orders, and responders rescued dozens of people, according to news reports , while water inundated streets and damaged property.
Heavy rain and flooding have been widespread across southwest Colorado, southeast Utah, northern Arizona, and northwest New Mexico in recent weeks. From early September through early November, precipitation totals were 2 to 4 times the average throughout the Four Corners region—an area beset by long-term drought that was exacerbated by snow drought and high temperatures in 2026.
Though the downpours posed hazards to communities along many rivers, they did provide drought relief throughout the region. Weekly U.S. Drought Monitor maps, derived from a suite of satellite data products and ground-based observations, have indicated improvements to drought conditions due to the fall storms. The group’s November 3 summary noted that “short-term drought has ended for the Southwest and Great Basin,” although long-term drought persists in places.
Wet weather in the Southwest is often associated with El Niño events, when the segment of the jet stream flowing eastward near the equatorial Pacific tends to strengthen. Experts noted that the low-pressure system delivering the heavy rainfall in autumn 2026 was at a low latitude for the time of year and drew energy from unusually high ocean temperatures. El Niño patterns—like the one currently underway —can increase the likelihood of moisture-laden storms being steered across the Southwest interior.
NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey . Story by Lindsey Doermann.

item.title: Has a Satellite Been Watching You?
item.summary: Have you ever wondered how many satellites have passed overhead while you've been going about your daily business? Probably quite a few. But how many of them were actually looking at you? Watched is an intriguing new interactive map which attempts to answer that question by revealing which satellites have passed over any location on Earth during the last seven days, and, more interestingly, which of them actually took a photograph. Visit Watched and enter any location in the world. The map will then reconstruct the satellite activity above that spot over the previous week, identifying the satellite that passed within viewing range and searching public satellite imagery archives for photographs captured during those passes. The result is a fascinating combination of satellite tracking, Earth observation imagery and a 3D globe. You can replay the satellite passes, watch their trajectories around the Earth and browse the photographs taken during each encounter. The globe even includes the positions of thousands of other tracked objects orbiting our planet, illuminated by the real position of the Sun. Not every satellite that passes overhead is necessarily taking a photograph, however.

item.title: Ships remain ablaze, oil supplies under threat as war turns Hormuz into maritime war zone
item.summary: An image captured by the European Union's Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellite on the same day showed a large plume of black smoke rising from the area.
item.page_text:
Market hopes of an Iran war de-escalation are colliding with a fresh wave of attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and energy infrastructure across the Middle East.
Crude prices hit two-month lows on Tuesday after US officials played down the need for further military action against Iran, with analysts pointing to President Donald Trump's more conciliatory tone since Republicans' defeat in the November 3 midterm elections.
But there has been little sign of attacks abating this month. A total of 37 ships were attacked in October, the highest monthly figure since the start of the war, according to data from the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
Videos posted on social media on Sunday and verified by Reuters showed the Navig8 Messi, a Singapore-flagged medium-sized refined products tanker, on fire off the coast of Oman. An image captured by the European Union's Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellite on the same day showed a large plume of black smoke rising from the area.
The vessel was among three tankers hit on Sunday for using "unauthorised routes" through the strait, Iranian state broadcaster IRIB reported, citing the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy.
Navig8, which manages the vessel and is majority-owned by ADNOC Logistics & Services, did not respond to Reuters requests for comment. ADNOC also did not reply.
Meanwhile, US forces continued enforcing a naval blockade of Iranian ports. In the latest incident, a US military aircraft fired on and disabled a St Kitts-flagged cargo vessel that attempted to leave regional waters after visiting an Iranian port on Saturday, US Central Command said.
The attacks have also raised environmental concerns, with damaged vessels leaking oil into surrounding waters. A video shared on social media on Monday and verified by Reuters showed oil reaching Oman's shoreline, while satellite imagery revealed spills off the coasts of Oman and the United Arab Emirates. The Omani government did not respond to a Reuters request for comment on the footage.
Elsewhere in the region, energy infrastructure and civilian facilities have also come under attack. Iranian forces and their regional allies have struck targets including the offices of Saudi Aramco, the world's largest oil company.
Video verified by Reuters showed damage to an Aramco office building in Riyadh following missile strikes claimed by Yemen's Houthi movement on November 8. Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry said the building had been targeted in an attempted attack, with falling debris causing limited damage. No injuries or fatalities were reported.
The maritime toll has continued to rise. The International Maritime Organisation (IMO) said it had recorded 133 confirmed incidents involving commercial vessels in the region as of November 10, with 25 seafarers killed since the conflict began. Thousands of crew members remain at risk, including those aboard ships unable to leave the Persian Gulf.
The IMO Council has called for stronger protection of seafarers and urged countries to avoid measures that could jeopardise the safety of international shipping.
In the latest reported incident, a tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile 19 nautical miles northeast of Oman's Lima on Tuesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said. Its crew were safe, and no environmental impact was reported.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy separately said two tankers had caught fire after striking naval mines while using what it described as an "unauthorised route" through the strait.

item.title: Tracking the Ocean’s Great Forest: How Hakai Institute's Kelp Explorer Is Helping British Columbia Secure Its Coastal Heritage
item.summary: The Kelp Explorer platform leverages Planet satellite imagery to help communities and organizations better understand and steward kelp forests.
item.page_text:
Kelp forest in Broughton Archipelago. Credit: Grant Callegari, Hakai Institute
This article was written in collaboration with the Hakai Institute. Co-authors at Planet include Thamires de Souza Ferreira and Cassidy Rankine.
At low tide on the west coast of Vancouver Island, bull kelp blades float on the ocean surface in a buoyant, sun-catching canopy. They sway in the Pacific swell in a kaleidoscope of golds, blues, and browns. For the people who look after Pacific Rim National Park Reserve , these kelp forests are more than beautiful scenery; they are nurseries for fish, food for sea otters, a buffer against storm surge, and one of the best barometers of nearshore ocean health. But despite the crucial and interconnected role they play in the ecosystem, they can be a challenge to measure and manage.
“For Parks Canada and the First Nations and local communities we work with, kelp is a key ecosystem in nearshore marine waters that supports biodiversity. Our job is to measure and monitor the health of these systems, and to understand if they’re improving, stable, or declining, and what that means for the park reserves,” says Pacific Rim National Park Reserve ecologist Jennifer Yakimishyn. “Because we can’t be underwater or everywhere at once, we’re looking for innovative methodologies to reflect those ecosystems by tracking kelp canopies.”
The Hakai Institute is harnessing Planet imagery to help Yakimishyn, and many others across British Columbia, solve this problem. They developed Kelp Explorer , an online platform designed to help communities and organizations better understand and steward these rich kelp forests.
For a seaweed that creates large canopies, kelp can be surprisingly hard to keep track of. Bull kelp is an annual macroalgae, so a kelp forest can grow, shrink, and move from one year to the next – even under healthy conditions. Tides hide and reveal the canopy several times a day. And in British Columbia, the coast is long, convoluted, and often under cloud, inhibiting a full accounting at scale.
Seventeen First Nations communities and the B.C. government know first-hand how much work it takes to comprehensively inventory. When they began building a regional kelp monitoring program under the Marine Plan Partnership for the North Pacific Coast , a group of Coastal Guardian Watchmen went out by boat to record kelp along roughly 800 linear kilometres of coastline, logging what they saw over the course of a summer.
Mamalilakulla Guardian Watchmen surveying Kelp by Kayak for a MaPP survey. Credit: Grant Callegari, Hakai Institute.
But the tides, capacity and shifting kelp have made it nearly impossible to repeat extensive, comprehensive boat-based surveys in a consistent way.
"It's very challenging to cover all that water and census hundreds of kilometers of coastline often enough to track kelp forests at those scales; we need other methods to help inform monitoring, research and management," says Luba Reshitnyk, who leads marine habitat mapping at Hakai Institute.
Marine protected areas across B.C. face this same problem. Gwaii Haanas, Pacific Rim, and Gulf Islands park reserves all have to report regularly on ecological indicators. While drone-based kelp forests surveys occur at local sites, data, methods and capacity are missing to map kelp forests across the whole managed region. Similarly, First Nations know how much kelp matters to their territories and heritage – as habitat that supports biodiversity, as a harvested and culturally important resource, and as an indicator of ecosystem health — and are looking for tools and resources to address the challenge of mapping and understanding kelp forests at large, regional scales.
Hakai Institute Research Scientist Luba Reshitnyk reviews data collected during a kelp monitoring survey on British Columbia’s Central Coast. Credit: Keith Holmes, Hakai Institute.
The Hakai Institute , part of the Tula Foundation , studies the B.C. coast, from its icefields to the deep ocean. Its geospatial team maps nearshore habitats using drones, aerial photography, lidar, and satellites, and creates specialized tools to help stakeholders address regional challenges and opportunities. In 2020, Hakai noted an important gap that deserved renewed attention: No one had surveyed where kelp grows along the B.C. coast, and how those forests are changing, since the mid-2000s. And no one had ever done it for the entire coast.
The team pulled together every dataset it could find or create. Building on drone-based, long-term monitoring site data which began in 2015, they embarked on regional scale species mapping using a fixed wing aircraft . For the deeper story, they used Landsat imagery to build a time series of the region with colleagues at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution and the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth . The analysis looks back decades, tracking change in expanse and location. It can identify outlier years, relating these shifts to marine heatwaves and other possible catalysts.
The team then used Planet imagery to provide a sharper lens. At about three-meter resolution, PlanetScope® picks up the small kelp beds that hug the shoreline, which other satellite sensors miss. It can give a fuller picture of the kelp forests that are there, and where changes affect local stakeholders. Machine learning models and pipelines built by Software Developer Taylor Denouden at Hakai classify Planet imagery at a scale beyond the scope of manual interpretation – visualizing this higher-resolution information across the region.
Visualization of kelp forests across the region, derived from PlanetScope data, analyzed by Hakai Institute and powering Kelp Explorer.
The result is Kelp Explorer , a free online tool designed to answer the big questions planners and communities have about kelp forests.
The design was shaped by many conversations with First Nations stewards and marine planners. "Remote sensing is pixels, and it's tricky to interpret," says Will Mc

item.page_text:
New geospatial AI capabilities are ready to help boost productivity and execute advanced spatial analytical workflows. Learn how to equip AI agents, such as Anthropic’s Claude or Microsoft Copilot Studio, with geospatial context, turn data and imagery into insights faster with AI premium services and embeddings, and bring trusted assistants across ArcGIS into your workflows. Let’s dive in.
We’re bringing AI and geography closer together in two ways.  First, we’re connecting ArcGIS to the agentic ecosystems your teams already use through MCP (Model Context Protocol), equipping AI agents like Anthropic’s Claude and Microsoft Copilot Studio, with foundational geospatial capabilities such as finding places, planning routes, and querying spatial data so they can answer location-related questions accurately. Second, we’re helping you make maps and data conversational so people across your organization can ask questions and get answers from your GIS content.
Any external AI agent can now be equipped with geospatial context, connecting to ArcGIS through MCP to understand where things are, search spatial data, and uncover what’s nearby or at risk. For example, in the demo below, you’ll see that you can get answers to questions like “which 5 assets within 0.25 miles should I inspect next? Prioritize them based on the last inspection date”.
Currently, MCP support in beta is available in ArcGIS Location Platform and ArcGIS Enterprise , with general availability coming later this year in their next respective releases. Existing ArcGIS maps, layers, and services can be leveraged by the agents that teams already use, augmenting those agents with geospatial context.
With or without code, your organization can now get answers from maps through conversation.
Developers can now build agentic mapping applications powered by out-of-the-box geospatial agents and custom agents you can create in both ArcGIS Enterprise 12.2 and ArcGIS Online using AI components (beta) in the ArcGIS Maps SDK for JavaScript . Users across your organization can interact with these custom mapping applications to find answers backed by geospatial data, asking questions like “How many counties produced less wheat in 2022 than in 2017?”.
In addition, a new out-of-the-box agent called knowledge agent is available in the AI components (beta) in the ArcGIS Maps SDK for JavaScript. You can ask questions of a knowledge graph service that can span many different relationships, such as “who are our top suppliers by spend” and get summarized answers with results visualized in a link chart or map. Ask follow-up questions to expand those results, find indirect paths between entities, and update the link chart directly from the chat, all without needing to write queries.
For teams that don’t want to code, start by creating a map with your data, then use the ArcGIS Instant Apps Data Explorer template (beta) to enhance it with a conversational experience. Available in ArcGIS Enterprise 12.2 and ArcGIS Online, the Data Explorer gives organizations a no-code way to create agentic mapping apps that let users across your organization interact with existing maps and data through natural language. Ask questions like “Show which fuel depots have less than two weeks of supply?” and other geospatially related inquiries to get answers faster.
You can also create agentic mapping applications with ArcGIS Experience Builder applications. Now available in beta in ArcGIS Online, AI chat lets users interact with configured ArcGIS Experience Builder apps through natural language, without rebuilding anything. App authors can enable AI chat in the app’s settings, and customize the chat name, style, tone, layout, and instructions to fit the app’s purpose. End users within your organization can interact with the app and access data through natural language to explore maps, find locations, run spatial queries, and print maps, all by describing a task.
AI tools and models, included with ArcGIS, accelerate how users create, extract, and analyze many types of geospatial data, including imagery, vector, text, time series, and 3D. In the release of ArcGIS Pro 3.8, we introduce a new foundation model, an embeddings dataset, and several AI tools that help users turn data into actionable insight.
Accelerate similarity search and predictive modeling across USA communities
The USA geodemographic embeddings 2026 layer is now in general availability. This dataset transforms demographic, socioeconomic, environmental, and census-derived variables, including data from the U.S. Census Bureau and American Community Survey (ACS), into embedding attributes that capture geodemographic and environmental characteristics across the United States. This helps analysts build more efficient workflows for predictive modeling, clustering, and similarity search for use cases like estimating health outcomes and identifying new market opportunities.
Earth observation foundation model turns multi-sensor imagery into insight
The earth observation foundation model (EO-DINO), developed by Esri, helps organizations extract information from remotely sensed imagery over a broad range of tasks with less labeled data. Trained using high-resolution RGB world imagery, multispectral satellite imagery, and SAR, EO-DINO captures fine-grained geographic details about the Earth across multiple sensors. Customers can access it as a deep learning package (.dlpk) in the ArcGIS Living Atlas and use it to identify similar features across large areas, detect changes, and differentiate Earth surface materials and land cover more accurately. This model generates geographic embeddings that work with analysis tools or works as a backbone for fine-tuning downstream models for environmental monitoring use cases and more.
